Oral medicine and dentistry · published research

Tooth extraction

Studies examine postoperative pain, swelling, jaw opening, soft-tissue recovery, and socket healing. Findings vary across extraction types, outcomes, and treatment protocols.

Evidence overview

Research on tooth extraction

Summary of the Evidence

The PBM Database lists 163 records related to tooth extraction, including 116 human reports, 23 animal-only studies (rat, rabbit, and dog), and one study with both human and rat arms. It also includes reviews and meta-analyses, protocols, and a cost analysis.

Clinical research mainly examines recovery after extraction, while animal studies investigate socket and tissue healing.

Human and clinical evidence

Randomized human studies mainly concern third-molar surgery and assess short-term pain, swelling, trismus, and healing. A scoping review included 22 randomized trials, with pain reported in 20 articles and clinical wound-healing outcomes in six (Sourvanos et al. 2023).

Individual trials show why outcomes should be considered separately. An 808-nm trial reported lower pain scores through 48 hours (Isolan et al. 2020), and another 808-nm split-mouth trial reported improvements in pain, swelling, and mouth opening (Sigaroodi et al. 2023). By contrast, adding 660-nm light to an 808-nm protocol did not improve most measured outcomes (de Paula et al. 2024). A more recent single-session extraoral trial reported early pain and quality-of-life differences but no edema or trismus effect (Anaç et al. 2026), while the multicenter BIOSTOTT trial found no significant benefit for its main postoperative outcomes (Giovannacci et al. 2026).

Animal evidence

The database includes 23 animal-only studies involving rats, rabbits, and dogs. In diabetic rats, both 660- and 808-nm light affected inflammation and vascularization, while improved osteoid formation was reported for the 808-nm protocol (Dalirsani et al. 2021).

A rabbit comparison found a beneficial bone-repair effect for LED treatment, but not a statistically significant laser-versus-control difference (Comunian et al. 2017). In a dog split-mouth model, repeated 980-nm treatment was associated with higher socket bone density at several follow-up points (Abdel Hamid et al. 2021). These studies examine healing in specific animal models and protocols.

Treatment Parameters and Generalizability

Human protocols vary substantially. Across 22 randomized trials, a scoping review found treatment times of 17 to 900 seconds per application and wavelengths from 550 to 1,064 nm in studies reporting postoperative pain. In studies reporting clinical wound healing, application times ranged from 30 to 120 seconds and wavelengths from 660 to 808 nm (Sourvanos et al. 2023).

Examples illustrate differences in dose and schedule. One 808-nm trial used a 50-mW laser at six points for about 74 seconds per point after extraction (Isolan et al. 2020). Another 808-nm trial applied light inside and outside the mouth after surgery and again 24 hours later (Sigaroodi et al. 2023). A split-mouth comparison applied 808-nm light alone or combined 660- and 808-nm light immediately after surgery and on days 3 and 7 (de Paula et al. 2024).

Other approaches include a single ten-minute extraoral treatment with 650- and 904-nm light (Anaç et al. 2026), LED protocols, and repeated animal treatments using 660, 808, or 980 nm (Dalirsani et al. 2021, Comunian et al. 2017, and Abdel Hamid et al. 2021). Wavelength, light source, dose, treated sites, timing, session frequency, and outcome measures all differ. The evidence describes a range of protocols, not a single established extraction regimen.

Interpretation

Human trials report positive findings for some outcomes and protocols, alongside null comparisons. The result of one regimen does not settle the effects of others. Current evidence is most informative when read by outcome, comparator, extraction procedure, and treatment schedule.

Further trials can clarify which protocols benefit which procedures by reporting treatment parameters in full and measuring pain, swelling, trismus, and healing over consistent follow-up periods.

Evidence strength in source summaryLow for early postoperative pain reduction with selected extraction protocolsVery low for consistent effects on swelling, trismus, or longer-term healing
Publications and records163 database records

Evidence strength rationale and next steps

Randomized trials report improvements in some settings, but they test different wavelengths, routes, schedules, extraction procedures, and outcomes. A scoping review also found a wide range of delivery times and wavelengths.

Future trials should compare clearly specified protocols and measure patient-important outcomes, including pain, swelling, jaw opening, and healing, using consistent follow-up.
